from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Formula: v_B equals P inverse v_A.", "P transforms new to old.", "Inverse converts old to new.", "A camera lens frame is new.", "Pixels map to world view."]
        self.setup_layout("The Change-of-Basis Formula", lecture_lines)
        
        # Elements
        formula = MathTex(r"[v]_B", "=", r"C^{-1}", r"[v]_A", font_size=48)
        C_matrix = MathTex(r"C", font_size=48, color="#FFA500")
        C_inv = MathTex(r"C^{-1}", font_size=48, color="#87CEFA")
        arrow = Arrow(start=self.grid['C4'], end=self.grid['C5'], color=WHITE)
        eq_sign = MathTex(r"=", font_size=48, color="#32CD32")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display the formula
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Color the change-of-basis matrix C in orange (#FFA500)
        # Assuming C is part of C_inv
        self.play(formula.animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFA500")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Flash the inverse matrix C^{-1} in light blue (#87CEFA)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#87CEFA")
        self.play(Indicate(formula[2])) # Highlight C^{-1}
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Animate an arrow
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(arrow, 'D3')
        self.play(GrowArrow(arrow))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Highlight the equality sign
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#32CD32")
        # Formula: [v]_B (0) = (1) C^{-1} (2) [v]_A (3)
        # The '=' sign is at index 1
        self.play(formula[1].animate.set_color("#32CD32"))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Summary & Conceptual Application", ["The vector itself never changes.", "Only its coordinate description shifts.", "Key for graphics and PCA."])
        
        # Setup visual elements
        axes_a = Axes(x_range=[-2, 2], y_range=[-2, 2], axis_config={"include_tip": True}).scale(0.5)
        axes_b = Axes(x_range=[-2, 2], y_range=[-2, 2], axis_config={"include_tip": True}).scale(0.5)
        vector = Arrow(ORIGIN, [1, 1, 0], color=YELLOW)
        
        group_a = VGroup(axes_a, vector.copy())
        group_b = VGroup(axes_b, vector.copy())
        
        self.place_at_grid(group_a, 'B2', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(group_b, 'B5', scale_factor=0.8)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#D3D3D3"))
        self.play(Create(group_a), Create(group_b))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#D3D3D3"))
        self.play(group_b.animate.rotate(PI/4))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#D3D3D3"))
        self.play(Indicate(group_a), Indicate(group_b))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Change of Basis in Linear Algebra

sections.title: Prerequisites & Intuition (1 Minute)
sections.content: Briefly define a basis as a 'coordinate system'. Use a 2D grid overlay to show that any vector can be reached using basis vectors (i, j). Introduce the core question: 'How do we describe the same physical vector if we change our perspective (basis)?'
sections.example: Visualize a treasure map where the 'grid' lines are rotated. Even if the grid changes, the 'X marks the spot' location in the world remains the same.

sections.title: The Mechanism of Coordinate Transformation (1.5 Minutes)
sections.content: Explain that a coordinate transformation is essentially mapping 'Old Coordinates' to 'New Coordinates' using a Change-of-Basis Matrix (P). Visualize P as columns of new basis vectors expressed in terms of the old basis.
sections.example: Imagine a robot dog moving in a square room. If the dog's local 'forward' direction changes, we use matrix P to translate its 'local' steps into the 'global' room coordinates.

sections.title: The Change-of-Basis Formula (1.5 Minutes)
sections.content: Formulate the equation: [v]_B = P_inv * [v]_A. Use animation to show the multiplication of the matrix against the vector. Emphasize that P represents the transformation from New to Old, so its inverse is required to convert Old to New.
sections.example: Use a camera analogy: The object is the vector. The 'Old Basis' is the world frame, and the 'New Basis' is the camera's lens frame. P allows the computer to calculate where pixels appear in the camera view.

sections.title: Summary & Conceptual Application (1 Minute)
sections.content: Conclude by emphasizing that the vector v is invariant—it doesn't change; only its description changes. Reiterate that this is the mathematical foundation for computer graphics (rotating objects) and data analysis (PCA).
sections.example: Final visual: A 3D character rotating in a game engine. Show how 'Change of Basis' is what allows the game to calculate the character's limbs relative to their own body, rather than the static game world.
